did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 65 opens with a heading identifying it as a psalm and song of David, for the director of music—meaning it was intended for musical performance or leadership.
Did you know? This verse presents silence itself as a form of praise to the Lord and adds that the vows made to him must be fulfilled.
Did you know? The Lord is described as the one who hears prayer, so the verse extends the appeal to him to all flesh—all people.
Did you know? The psalm includes a personal confession of sin: iniquities overwhelm us, but the Lord atones for the people’s transgressions.

Did you know? The happiness described in this chapter is connected with closeness to the Lord: the blessed person is the one whom the Lord chooses and draws near, who dwells in his courts and is satisfied with the goodness of his house.
Did you know? The Lord is presented as the source of salvation and security not only for Israel, but also for all the ends of the earth and the distant shores of the sea.
Did you know? The Lord’s power is described as preparing and establishing the mountains, making creation itself a testimony to his might.
Did you know? The psalm attributes to the Lord control both over the roaring of the seas and their waves and over the tumult of the nations—over turmoil in nature and chaos among humanity.
Did you know? The Lord’s signs inspire awe among the inhabitants of the ends of the earth, while the rising of morning and evening is described as a source of joyful song.
Did you know? The final part of the psalm describes the blessing of the land: the Lord visits it, waters it, and enriches it, and the streams prepare the grain for growth.
